strings.title: Unit Fractions Add Up
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Adding the same unit fraction again and again is multiplying: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 is 3 × 1/4, which is 3/4.
strings.keywords: unit fraction, repeated addition, groups of, fourths, fifths, thirds, numerator
watchFor: Multiplying the denominator too (3 × 1/4 = 3/12): ask "Three fourths, or three twelfths? Count the jumps."
Adding denominators (1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8): ask "Did the pieces change size?"
Not seeing 5/5 or 4/4 as a whole: ask "How many fifths make one whole?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How is 3 × 1/4 the same as 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4?" Land: both count three fourths. The number of unit fractions is the numerator, and the size of the piece doesn't change.

problems.notes: Look for: counting fourths: one fourth, two fourths, three fourths. Ask: "What are we counting?" Word choice: say "one fourth", not "one over four". Model: numberline +1/4 +1/4 +1/4

responses.tip: The target idea: counting unit fractions.
Added the denominators. Ask: did the pieces get smaller?

problems.notes: Look for: the same as the last one. Ask: "Why is it the same?" Model: numberline +1/4 +1/4 +1/4

responses.say: 3 groups of 1/4 is 3/4, just like the last one.
responses.tip: Ask: how is × the same as adding again?
Multiplied the denominator. Ask: count the jumps of 1/4.

problems.notes: Look for: four fifths. Ask: "How many more fifths to make a whole?" Model: numberline +1/5 +1/5 +1/5 +1/5
Look for: five fifths is a whole. Ask: "What's another name for 5/5?" Model: numberline +1/5 +1/5 +1/5 +1/5 +1/5

responses.tip: Ask: how many fifths make a whole?

problems.notes: Look for: one more fifth past the whole: 6/5 or 1 1/5. Ask: "Can a fraction be more than 1?" Model: numberline +1/5 +1/5 +1/5 +1/5 +1/5 +1/5

responses.say: 5 fifths is 1, plus one more fifth.

problems.notes: Look for: 3 thirds make 1, 2 more thirds. Ask: "Where is 1 on the number line?" Model: numberline +1/3 +1/3 +1/3 +1/3 +1/3

responses.tip: Ask: is 5 thirds more or less than 1?

problems.notes: Look for: 4 fourths is 1, 8 fourths is 2. Ask: "How many wholes?" Model: numberline +1/4x8

strings.title: Counting Unit Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Count unit fractions like counting anything else: 4 × 1/3 is four thirds. When the count passes a whole, it's more than 1.
strings.keywords: unit fraction, repeated addition, thirds, fourths, tenths, halves, more than a whole
watchFor: Multiplying the denominator (4 × 1/3 = 4/12): ask "Four thirds, or four twelfths? Count the jumps."
Thinking a fraction can't be more than 1: ask "Where is 4/3 on the number line?"
Not seeing 10/10 as 1: ask "How many tenths make a whole?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How do you know when the count passes 1?" Land: when the number of pieces is more than the number in a whole (more than 3 thirds), the total is more than 1.

problems.notes: Look for: four thirds, past the whole. Ask: "How many thirds make a whole?" Word choice: say "four thirds". Model: numberline +1/3 +1/3 +1/3 +1/3

responses.tip: Added the denominators. Ask: did the pieces get smaller?

problems.notes: Look for: the same as the last one. Ask: "Why is it the same?" Model: numberline +1/3 +1/3 +1/3 +1/3
Look for: 4 fourths make 1, 3 more fourths. Ask: "Where is 1?" Model: numberline +1/4x7

responses.tip: Both 7/4 and 1 3/4 are right. x7 means 7 jumps of 1/4.

problems.notes: Look for: 10 tenths is 1. Ask: "How many tenths in a whole?" Model: numberline +1/10x10

responses.tip: Ask: count the tenths. How many make a whole?

problems.notes: Look for: 1 whole and 2 tenths, like 1.2. Ask: "How is this like decimals?" Model: numberline +1/10x12

responses.tip: Decimals connection. x12 means 12 jumps of 1/10.

problems.notes: Look for: 9 halves: 4 wholes and a half. Ask: "How many halves in each whole?" Model: numberline +1/2x9
Look for: 5 fifths in each whole: 3 wholes. Ask: "How many wholes?" Model: numberline +1/5x15
